report:
**Conclusion: The evidence overall does not support ginkgo extract as an effective treatment for tinnitus.** Your answer (“no”) aligns with the conclusions of major systematic reviews and clinical guidelines, though some individual trials report modest benefits in selected patients.

**Evidence against efficacy (stronger):**
- The Cochrane systematic review found few good-quality trials and concluded there was no reliable evidence that Ginkgo biloba reduces tinnitus severity compared with placebo (four trials, 1,543 participants) [1].
- A review in the American Academy of Family Physicians notes that ginkgo is “probably not effective” for tinnitus, with proposed mechanisms (vasoregulation, neuronal metabolism) not translating into clinical benefit [2].
- Current European and American tinnitus guidelines recommend against using ginkgo biloba for tinnitus [3].

**Evidence suggesting possible benefit (weaker):**
- A systematic review of randomized, placebo-controlled trials reported evidence of efficacy for the standardized extract EGb 761® in tinnitus, but only from three trials in patients with tinnitus related to underlying vascular or cognitive conditions; results across preparations and populations were mixed [4].

**Bottom line:** While ginkgo is widely prescribed and some small studies suggest limited benefit in specific subgroups, the highest-quality evidence—Cochrane review and clinical guidelines—does not support its routine use to relieve tinnitus symptoms.

**Sources:**
[1] https://www.cochrane.org/hr/evidence/CD003852_ginkgo-biloba-tinnitus  
[2] https://www.racgp.org.au/afp/2015/august/your-questions-about-complementary-medicines-answe  
[3] https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6926930/  
[4] https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3157487/
